name: Red light LED mask
lead: A red light LED mask is a wearable or handheld panel that delivers red light, and often near-infrared light, to the face for a few minutes per session. The technology is a consumer form of low-level light therapy, also called photobiomodulation (PBM), which applies low-power lasers or LEDs without damaging tissue.[1][3][11] Typical marketed wavelengths fall in the red (about 620-700 nm) and near-infrared (about 700-1440 nm) ranges.[2][3]

Masks are sold for fine lines, skin tone and texture, and recovery after procedures. A 2024 dermatology continuing-education review states that PBM is used effectively for conditions including acne, skin rejuvenation, wounds, scars and alopecia and describes it as having a favourable safety profile.[4] Home-device trials are fewer; a multicentre, randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled study of a home LED and infrared mask for crow's feet was published in 2025, and a split-face pilot of a 637 and 854 nm home LED device appeared in 2020.[5][6]
Reviewers note that devices vary widely in wavelength and dose, and that trial sizes are modest and sometimes industry-linked.[4]

paras: Masks arrange LEDs across a face-shaped shell, while panels and wands are held at a distance. Many combine red (roughly 630-660 nm) and near-infrared (roughly 800-850 nm) diodes. Several photobiomodulation devices are cleared by the US FDA, according to Wikipedia's article on low-level laser therapy.[11]

Wikipedia credits Niels Finsen, who received the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, as the father of modern light therapy; he used red light for smallpox lesions.[11] The Hungarian physician Endre Mester discovered biological effects of low-power lasers after the invention of the ruby laser in 1960 and the helium-neon laser in 1961; in a faulty-laser experiment on mice, shaved areas regrew hair faster, which he published in 1967.[11] He later reported accelerated wound healing and called the approach laser biostimulation, a term later superseded by low-level laser therapy and photobiomodulation.[11]

By 1987 companies selling lasers were claiming treatments for pain, sports injuries and arthritis with little supporting evidence, according to the same source, and in 2014 the FDA filed a complaint against one manufacturer, QLaser, for marketing devices for over 200 diseases; a permanent injunction followed in 2015.[11] LED masks for cosmetic use are a later consumer development of the same technology.

Photobiomodulation theory holds that light must be absorbed to act, and the generally accepted candidate is cytochrome c oxidase in the mitochondrial respiratory chain.[11] A 2024 review describes red and near-infrared absorption by this enzyme as modulating mitochondrial ATP, reactive oxygen species and intracellular calcium, which in turn activate signalling pathways such as those involving insulin-like growth factor.[2] In skin, this is proposed to stimulate fibroblasts to produce collagen and to reduce inflammation.[2] Wikipedia notes that doses below an effective range do not appear to work, and that effects seem limited to certain wavelengths.[11]

A 2024 dermatology review states that PBM can be effective in acne, rejuvenation, wounds and scars among other conditions.[4] Evidence for home masks is narrower. A 2025 multicentre, randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial examined a home LED and infrared mask for crow's feet.[5] The 2020 split-face pilot tested a home LED device at 637 and 854 nm for facial rejuvenation.[6] A 2023 article in Skin Research and Technology discussed red-light PBM and signs of skin aging.[12] Authors of this literature commonly note small samples, short follow-up and variable dosing, and trial results suggest subtle rather than dramatic changes.[4][5]

Wikipedia reports mild pain or skin irritation after red-light therapy and states that long-term effects on skin or hair are not known; eye protection is suggested for some devices.[11] A 2023 systematic review in Aesthetic Surgery Journal assessed the oncologic safety of low-level light therapy for aesthetic rejuvenation, and Wikipedia summarises a systematic review finding no evidence that people with cancer or at risk of cancer should avoid PBM.[7][11] Clinical guidelines cited there suggest consulting a dermatologist first and using devices authorised by the relevant regulator.[11]

Repeated low-level red-light therapy has been studied extensively for slowing myopia in children. A multicentre randomized trial of 264 children aged 8 to 13, a trial in high-myopia children, a double-blind sham-controlled trial of 112 children, and a network meta-analysis of atropine, orthokeratology and red light are among the reports.[8][9][10][13] These use specialised low-power laser devices under clinical supervision and do not evaluate cosmetic masks.

Human studies of home masks include a 2025 multicentre, double-blind, sham-controlled trial for crow's feet[5] and a 2020 split-face pilot study at 637 and 854 nm.[6] Professional-device and review literature for acne, wound healing and rejuvenation is summarised in dermatology reviews.[4][2] Research on myopia and other conditions is a separate use and is not evidence about facial appearance.[8][9]
